Can You Get Dental Implants If You Have a Genetic Connective Tissue Disorder Like Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

If you live with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (EDS) or another genetic connective tissue disorder, you may have already learned to approach medical decisions with extra care. When it comes to missing teeth and exploring tooth replacement options, many patients understandably wonder whether dental implants are a safe and realistic option for them.

Searching online for answers about dental implants and Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome is entirely understandable — but the information available is often scattered, overly technical, or written without considering the specific concerns of patients with complex medical backgrounds.

This article aims to explain, in clear and balanced terms, how genetic connective tissue disorders like EDS may influence dental implant candidacy, what factors a dental professional will consider during assessment, and what questions are worth raising at a consultation. It also provides context around oral health management for people living with EDS more broadly.

Please note that this article is educational in nature. Only a qualified dental professional can determine whether dental implants are clinically appropriate for you following a thorough individual examination.

Can You Get Dental Implants With Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome?

Dental implants may be possible for some people with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome, but suitability depends on individual clinical assessment. Factors such as bone density, tissue integrity, healing capacity, and systemic health must all be carefully evaluated. A detailed dental consultation is essential to determine whether dental implants are appropriate for each patient with EDS.

What Is Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and How Does It Affect the Body?

Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome is a group of inherited connective tissue disorders caused by defects in the structure, production, or processing of collagen — a protein that provides strength and elasticity to the body's tissues. There are 13 recognised subtypes of EDS, each with varying characteristics, though the most common is hypermobile EDS (hEDS).

Because collagen is found throughout the body — in skin, joints, blood vessels, tendons, and ligaments — EDS can affect multiple systems simultaneously. Common features across subtypes include hypermobile joints, skin that is more fragile or elastic than usual, and a tendency for tissues to heal more slowly or differently after injury or surgery.

From a dental perspective, the implications of EDS are significant. Collagen plays a fundamental role in the health of the gums, the periodontal ligament (the tissue that anchors teeth to the jawbone), and the structural integrity of the jawbone itself. Understanding these relationships is essential when evaluating whether dental implants are appropriate for a patient with EDS.

It is also worth noting that EDS can present very differently between individuals — even within the same subtype — so any clinical evaluation must be highly personalised.

How Does EDS Specifically Affect Oral Health?

People with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome often experience a range of oral health challenges that may be more pronounced than in the general population. These are not universal to every person with EDS, but they are worth being aware of.

Gum fragility and periodontal concerns: Because collagen supports the gum tissue and the periodontal ligament, EDS-related collagen abnormalities may contribute to more fragile gum tissue, a higher susceptibility to gum recession, and in some cases an increased risk of periodontal (gum) disease.

Temporomandibular joint (TMJ) issues: Joint hypermobility in EDS can extend to the temporomandibular joint — the joint connecting the jaw to the skull. This can lead to jaw pain, clicking, locking, and difficulty with bite function.

Dentinogenesis and enamel concerns: Some research suggests that certain EDS subtypes may be associated with abnormalities in dentin or enamel formation, which can make teeth more susceptible to damage over time.

Delayed or atypical healing: Collagen is essential to the wound-healing process. Patients with EDS may experience slower or different wound healing following dental procedures, which is a clinically important consideration.

Medication interactions: Many people with EDS manage chronic pain or other systemic symptoms with medications that may have oral health implications, including dry mouth or increased bleeding risk. Related systemic considerations are also discussed in this guide on how autoimmune diseases can affect implant success.

The Clinical Science: Why Collagen Matters for Dental Implant Success

To understand why EDS is relevant to dental implant candidacy, it helps to understand what osseointegration is and why it matters.

A dental implant is a small titanium post that is surgically placed into the jawbone to act as an artificial tooth root. For an implant to be successful long-term, it must undergo a process called osseointegration — where the surrounding bone tissue grows around and bonds directly to the surface of the implant. This process typically takes several months and depends on healthy bone density, adequate blood supply, and efficient tissue healing.

The surrounding soft tissues — primarily the gum tissue — must also heal effectively around the implant and the abutment (the connector piece that sits above the gum line). Healthy collagen production underpins both bone regeneration and soft tissue healing.

In patients with EDS, several collagen-related factors may potentially influence implant outcomes:

  • Reduced tissue tensile strength may affect how gum tissue seals around the implant site
  • Slower or atypical wound healing can extend recovery timelines and may increase infection risk if not carefully managed
  • Bone quality variations — although EDS primarily affects soft connective tissue, some research indicates potential secondary effects on bone matrix quality
  • Vascular EDS (vEDS), a rarer but more serious subtype, involves significant blood vessel fragility and may present particular surgical risks

None of these factors automatically disqualifies a patient from receiving dental implants. However, they do mean that a detailed and multi-disciplinary assessment is essential — ideally involving both the dental team and the patient's managing physician or specialist.

Factors a Dentist Will Assess Before Recommending Implants

When a dentist evaluates a patient with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome for dental implants, the assessment will typically be more involved than a standard implant consultation. The following factors are among those a clinician will consider:

Bone volume and density: Dental X-rays and, where appropriate, a CBCT (cone beam computed tomography) scan will help determine whether there is sufficient bone to support an implant safely.

Periodontal health: Any existing gum disease must be identified and brought under control before implant treatment can be considered. Gum disease is a common cause of implant failure even in patients without systemic conditions.

Healing history: A clinician will want to understand how the patient has healed following previous dental or medical procedures. Slow healing, excessive scarring, or wound breakdown are all relevant clinical factors.

Subtype of EDS: The specific subtype of EDS a patient has will influence the risk profile. Vascular EDS, for example, would require particularly careful multi-disciplinary consideration due to blood vessel fragility.

Current medications: Anticoagulants, anti-inflammatory medications, immunosuppressants, and other drugs may influence surgical risk or healing.

Overall systemic health: Conditions frequently associated with EDS — such as dysautonomia, mast cell activation syndrome (MCAS), or anxiety — may also need to be factored into treatment planning.

For patients exploring their options, a dental implant consultation is an important first step in understanding individual suitability.

Are Dental Implants Completely Off the Table for EDS Patients?

The short answer is: not necessarily — but it genuinely depends on the individual.

Some patients with EDS may be well-suited to dental implants, particularly those with well-controlled oral health, adequate bone volume, and no contraindications related to their specific subtype or medications. With careful planning, appropriate surgical technique, and diligent post-operative care, implants may offer a functional and long-lasting tooth replacement solution.

For other patients, the risks associated with healing, tissue integrity, or surgical complexity may mean that alternative tooth replacement options — such as implant-retained dentures, bridges, or other prosthetic solutions — are more appropriate and achievable outcomes.

It is also worth considering that EDS affects each person differently. Two people with the same EDS subtype may have quite different clinical profiles and, consequently, different treatment suitability.

This is why any decision about dental implants must be made collaboratively between the patient and the dental team, ideally with input from the patient's wider medical team where relevant. There are no blanket answers — only individual assessments.

Alternative Tooth Replacement Options Worth Understanding

If dental implants are not immediately suitable for a patient with EDS, it is helpful to know that other tooth replacement options exist. A dental professional can explain each option in the context of the patient's specific oral health and systemic health circumstances.

Conventional dentures: Removable full or partial dentures do not require surgical intervention and may be appropriate for patients for whom implant surgery carries too high a risk. However, they can sometimes affect gum tissue and bone over time.

Implant-retained dentures: In some cases, even patients with complex medical histories may be suitable for a reduced number of implants to help stabilise a denture, rather than full individual implants for each missing tooth. This reduces surgical burden while improving prosthetic stability.

Dental bridges: A fixed bridge supported by adjacent natural teeth can restore the appearance and function of missing teeth without surgical implant placement. This option depends on the health and suitability of the neighbouring teeth.

Each of these options carries its own clinical considerations, and suitability depends on individual assessment. Patients with EDS are encouraged to ask their dental team to discuss all available options during consultation. You can learn more about the range of implant treatment options available to help you prepare informed questions.

Maintaining Oral Health When Living With EDS

Regardless of whether dental implants are ultimately suitable, maintaining excellent oral health is particularly important for people with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome. The systemic effects of EDS can create a higher baseline risk for certain dental issues, so proactive oral care is worthwhile.

Regular dental check-ups: Attending routine dental appointments allows any emerging issues — such as gum recession, tooth wear, or early signs of decay — to be identified and addressed promptly. More frequent hygiene appointments may be recommended by your dentist.

Gentle oral hygiene practices: For those with EDS-related gum fragility, overly vigorous brushing can cause trauma. A soft-bristled toothbrush and gentle technique are generally advisable, alongside flossing or interdental brushing as recommended by your dental team.

Managing dry mouth: If medications or systemic conditions contribute to dry mouth (xerostomia), addressing this is important, as saliva plays a key role in protecting teeth from decay. Sugar-free gum, adequate hydration, and specific oral rinses may help.

Monitoring for jaw joint symptoms: Because TMJ issues are relatively common in EDS, reporting jaw pain, clicking, or limited mouth opening to your dentist early allows for prompt assessment and management.

Communicating your medical history fully: Always ensure your dental team has a complete and up-to-date understanding of your diagnosis, current medications, and any relevant systemic concerns. This allows them to adapt treatment safely.

When to Seek a Professional Dental Assessment

If you have Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome and are experiencing any of the following, it is worth arranging a dental assessment sooner rather than later:

  • Loose or missing teeth that are affecting your ability to eat, speak, or maintain confidence
  • Gum recession, bleeding gums, or gum discomfort that has not been recently reviewed
  • Jaw pain, clicking, or locking that is affecting your daily life
  • Dental pain, swelling, or discomfort of any kind
  • Concerns about existing dental restorations or the condition of your teeth

Equally, if you are simply at the stage of exploring tooth replacement options and want to understand whether dental implants might be suitable for you, arranging a consultation is entirely appropriate. There is no pressure to commit to treatment — a consultation is simply an opportunity to ask questions and receive personalised information from a qualified professional.

It is worth asking your dental provider specifically about their experience in managing patients with systemic conditions, as a thoughtful and well-informed approach to your care is important. Reviewing what to expect at a dental implant consultation can help you feel more prepared before attending.

Key Points to Remember

  • Dental implants may be possible for some people with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome, but individual suitability must be determined through thorough clinical assessment.
  • EDS affects collagen throughout the body, including in the gums, periodontal ligament, and jawbone — all of which are relevant to dental implant success.
  • The specific EDS subtype matters — vascular EDS, for example, carries different surgical risk considerations than hypermobile EDS.
  • Alternative tooth replacement options exist and may be appropriate for patients where implants are not clinically indicated.
  • Regular dental care and open communication with your dental team are especially important when living with a connective tissue disorder.
  • No online article can determine treatment suitability — only a qualified dental professional conducting a clinical examination can assess your individual situation.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is there evidence that dental implants fail more often in people with EDS?

Robust large-scale clinical studies specifically examining implant success rates in EDS patients are currently limited. Some case reports and smaller studies suggest that certain EDS-related factors — such as atypical tissue healing and gum fragility — may present challenges. However, outcomes vary considerably between individuals. A thorough pre-treatment assessment, careful surgical planning, and diligent aftercare can help optimise outcomes for appropriate candidates. Your dental team will discuss realistic expectations based on your personal clinical profile.

Does EDS affect the jawbone in a way that would prevent implants?

EDS primarily affects soft connective tissues rather than bone directly. However, secondary effects on bone quality or density are occasionally noted in research, and some EDS patients may have received long-term medications that affect bone metabolism. Bone volume and quality will be carefully evaluated using dental imaging at your consultation. Bone grafting procedures may sometimes be recommended to optimise implant site preparation where bone is insufficient.

Can EDS cause tooth loss?

EDS is not a direct cause of tooth loss in the way that dental decay or gum disease is. However, the oral health challenges associated with EDS — including gum fragility, possible enamel changes, and TMJ-related occlusal issues — can increase the risk of dental problems over time if oral health is not carefully maintained. Addressing oral health proactively and attending regular dental appointments can help minimise this risk.

Should I tell my dentist about my EDS diagnosis before any dental treatment?

Absolutely. Disclosing your full medical history — including your EDS diagnosis, subtype if known, all current medications, and any relevant systemic conditions — is essential before any dental treatment. This information helps your dental team adapt their approach appropriately, plan anaesthesia and sedation safely, and anticipate any healing or procedural considerations. Being open with your dental team is always in your best interest.

Are there specific EDS subtypes where dental implants are more likely to be contraindicated?

Vascular EDS (vEDS) is the subtype where surgical procedures — including dental implants — require particularly careful multi-disciplinary consideration, due to the risk of blood vessel fragility and the potential for surgical complications. Patients with vEDS should ensure their dental team is fully informed and, where appropriate, that treatment is coordinated with their medical specialists. Other subtypes carry varying risk profiles. A clinical consultation will help clarify what your specific situation entails.

How can I find a dentist experienced in treating patients with complex medical conditions?

When booking a consultation, it is entirely appropriate to ask whether the practice has experience in managing patients with systemic or connective tissue conditions. You may also wish to share relevant clinical information in advance — such as your EDS subtype, any guidelines from EDS UK or your medical team, and a list of your current medications. A well-informed, patient-centred dental team will welcome this information and use it to support the planning of your care.

Conclusion

Living with Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome brings unique challenges, and navigating decisions about dental treatment — including whether dental implants are suitable — requires a careful, well-informed approach. Dental implants and Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome are not inherently incompatible, but the relationship between EDS-related collagen changes and the biological processes that support implant success means that individual assessment is absolutely essential.

For some patients with EDS, dental implants may offer an excellent long-term tooth replacement solution. For others, alternative options may be more appropriate based on their specific clinical profile. The only way to determine which category you fall into is through an honest, thorough conversation with a qualified dental professional who has access to your full medical and dental history.

Maintaining good oral health, attending regular dental check-ups, and communicating openly with your dental team are meaningful steps you can take right now — regardless of where you are in your tooth replacement journey.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.
